title: The f7 Attack (Scholar's Mate)
idea: f7 is the only square in Black's camp defended by nothing but the king. White's fastest cheap plan is to aim two pieces at it — a bishop on c4 and the queen — and mate before Black develops. Your job is not to memorise a refutation. It is to notice the double attack the moment the second attacker arrives, and to answer it with a move that also does something useful: gains a tempo on the queen, or develops a piece. Meet it correctly and White has an exposed queen, no development, and a lost opening.

cues.text: A white bishop lands on c4. It is already aiming at f7.
The white queen goes to h5 or f3. Now two pieces hit f7 and only your king defends it.
White has moved the queen early and developed nothing else. Every move you make that hits the queen is a free tempo.

recognition.prompt: White has just played the queen to h5. What is actually happening?

choices.why: The queen on h5 and the bishop on c4 both hit f7, and only your king defends it — he cannot take the queen because the bishop guards her.

choices.text: The e5 pawn is attacked and will fall
choices.why: The queen does attack e5, but your knight on c6 defends it. That is not the problem.

choices.text: Nothing — the queen is just badly placed
choices.why: The queen IS badly placed, which is why this whole line is bad for White. But the threat is real: ignore it and the game ends.

choices.text: White threatens to trap the knight on c6

plan.goal: Never let f7 be attacked more times than it is defended.
Every defensive move should also develop a piece or hit the queen.
Keep the king able to castle. Do not solve this by pushing the f- or h-pawn.

line.threat: Qxf7 is mate. f7 is attacked by the queen and the bishop, and defended only by the king — who cannot recapture, because the bishop on c4 guards f7.
hints: Something in your position is attacked twice and defended once. Find it before you consider anything else.
You can block the attacker's path or add a defender. One of those choices also kicks the queen, which wins you a move.
The move that blocks and gains a tempo is a kingside pawn move.

moves.why: Blocks the h5–f7 diagonal and attacks the queen at the same time, so White must move her again. You defend and gain a tempo in one move — that is why this is the main line.
The queen steps onto the f-file and renews exactly the same threat on f7. Nothing has changed for you. Recognise it again.

then.threat: The same threat from a new square. Qxf7 is still mate: the queen on f3 and the bishop on c4 both hit f7.
hints: White repeated the idea from a different square. Ask yourself the same question you asked last move.
This time the queen attacks along the f-file rather than the diagonal. Block the file.
The blocking move is also your most natural developing move.

moves.why: Now this is right. It blocks the f-file, develops, and takes a square the queen wanted. The same move that lost on move three wins on move four — the difference is whether the diagonal or the file is the problem.
White finally develops a piece, which is the admission that the attack is over.

terminal.summary: Threat neutralised — now count the position instead of the moves. You have two minor pieces out, a fianchetto coming and a king that can castle. White has a bishop, a knight, and a queen that spent three moves going nowhere. You are better, and not because you memorised anything: every move you spent on defence also developed a piece or kicked the queen, while White moved the same piece over and over.

moves.why: Defends f7 again. Solid, but you are spending queen moves on defence while your pieces sit at home.
Defends f7 and offers a queen trade, which is fine for you — trading queens kills White's entire plan. The cost is that your knight loses its best square.

mistakes.why: The trap inside the trap. It looks wonderful — you hit the queen and c2 at once — but it does nothing about f7, and your own queen on d8 is covering her king's only flight square.
Fianchettoing is the right long-term idea and the wrong move right now. It does not touch f7.

moves.why: Adds a defender to f7, which is enough. The cost is that your queen now blocks the f8 bishop, so development gets awkward.
Defends f7 and eyes f2. Playable, but your queen takes the square your knight wants.
The knight does cover f7, so you survive — but Bxh6 wrecks the pawns in front of the king you were about to castle toward. You solved the tactic and bought a long-term weakness.

mistakes.why: The most common losing move in club chess. A perfectly normal developing move that develops straight into mate, because it does nothing about f7.
Opens your bishop and defends e5 — but the threat was never about e5. f7 is still attacked twice and defended once.
Develops with an attack on f2. You are counting on a race you have already lost: White is one move faster.
